approach: Find the maximum static friction from the push force, then compare it with the resultant of gravity and the parallel force to see if the block can stay still.

steps.text: The wall's normal reaction equals the push force, so find the maximum static friction it can provide.
steps.equation: R = 20 N, f(max static) = μₛR = 0.25×20 = 5 N

steps.text: Gravity (10 N, downward) and the second 10 N force (horizontal, along the wall) both lie in the plane of the wall and are perpendicular to each other.
Find the resultant of these two forces, which is what friction would need to balance for the block to stay still.
Since 14.1 N is greater than the maximum available friction of 5 N, the block slides, moving along the direction of this resultant.
steps.equation: resultant direction is 45° from the vertical, toward the 10 N force

final_answer.value: The block moves, sliding along the resultant of gravity and the 10 N force, at 45° from the vertical.

common_mistakes.text: Adding the two 10 N forces (gravity and the applied force) directly instead of combining them as perpendicular vectors gives 20 N instead of 10√2 N ≈ 14.1 N.

Comparing only the applied 10 N force with the maximum friction of 5 N, ignoring gravity, still concludes the block moves but with the wrong direction, along the applied force alone rather than at 45°.
